name: Tibolone (Livial)

lead: Tibolone is a prescription hormone therapy for menopause symptoms and osteoporosis in many countries, though not the US. Some bodybuilding forum posters discuss it as a mild anabolic with a possible lean-mass effect.

It is a prodrug whose metabolites act on estrogen, progesterone and androgen receptors in tissue-selective ways and lower SHBG. It has been tested in large randomised trials for menopause symptoms and bone; no study has tested it for appearance or muscle.

paras: Medically it is a daily oral tablet for postmenopausal women. In muscle contexts it is mentioned as a milder add-on rather than a main compound.

Trials and reviews report increased stroke risk in older women, higher breast cancer recurrence in survivors, and endometrial and bleeding concerns. Acne and facial hair occur in some women. It is a Canadian Schedule IV controlled substance and banned by WADA.

angle.text: Tibolone is a menopause drug that some users discuss as a mild anabolic for lean mass, via weak androgenic activity. It has been trialled extensively for menopause symptoms and bone, but not for looks.

lead: Tibolone, sold as Livial and under other brand names, is an oral synthetic steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity, classed as a selective tissue estrogenic activity regulator (STEAR). It is prescribed to postmenopausal women for hot flushes, vaginal atrophy and prevention of osteoporosis [1][2].

It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in the Netherlands in 1988 and the UK in 1991. It is not approved in the United States, is a Canadian Schedule IV controlled substance because it is classed as an anabolic steroid, and is prohibited by WADA [1][2].

Large randomised trials and observational studies have examined its benefits and risks in menopausal women [3][4][5]. No studies were found of tibolone for appearance or physique in men or women, though its androgenic activity and anabolic-steroid classification explain why it is mentioned in muscle-related contexts.
infobox: Synthetic steroid; STEAR (prodrug of estrogenic and androgenic metabolites)
Rx (UK, Australia); Schedule IV (Canada); not available in US; WADA-prohibited

paras: Tibolone is indicated for menopausal vasomotor and urogenital symptoms and for prevention of osteoporosis in women at risk of fractures who cannot use other therapies [1][2]. It has also been studied for sexual function and mood in postmenopausal women [1][2].

Tibolone itself is inactive; it is converted to 3-alpha- and 3-beta-hydroxytibolone (estrogenic) and the delta-4 isomer (progestogenic and androgenic). Tissue-selective activity gives effects on bone, brain and vagina with less stimulation of the uterus and breast [1][6]. Wikipedia reports a half-life of about 45 hours and a roughly 50 percent reduction in SHBG [1].

Androgenic effects such as acne and facial hair occur in a minority of women, and unscheduled bleeding is common [1]. A 2016 Cochrane review linked tibolone to higher rates of stroke, cardiovascular events and endometrial cancer, though much of the evidence was low quality; breast cancer findings have been mixed [1]. Contraindications include breast cancer, thromboembolic disease and undiagnosed vaginal bleeding [2].

The LIFT trial randomised 4,538 women aged 60 to 85 with osteoporosis to tibolone or placebo and examined fractures, breast cancer and cardiovascular events [3]; it was reported to show fewer vertebral fractures and breast cancers, alongside an increased stroke risk. The LIBERATE trial (n = 3,148) in women with a history of breast cancer examined recurrence and symptom relief and reported a higher recurrence rate with tibolone [4][7]. The Million Women Study observational data on hormone therapy included tibolone in analyses of breast and endometrial cancer [5][8]. Smaller trials have looked at HDL cholesterol, vascular function, bone density versus raloxifene, and menopausal depression [9][10]. No studies were found of tibolone for appearance or muscle.

Tibolone's classification as an anabolic steroid in Canada and its WADA prohibition are the main links to athletic contexts [1]. The FDA did not authorise it in the US after 2006 on safety grounds, according to Grokipedia [2].
